name: Amazon Athena
summary: AWS’s serverless SQL engine for data in S3: no cluster to run, and on-demand queries cost $5 per TB scanned.
intro: You define tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, pointing at files in S3, and run SQL from the console, the API or a JDBC or ODBC driver. AWS supplies the compute for each query and takes it away when the query ends. On demand, you pay $5 for every TB a query scans, so converting data to compressed Parquet and partitioning it cuts the bill directly. For steady workloads, Capacity Reservations charge $0.30 per DPU-hour instead.

Athena engine version 3 continuously integrates open-source Trino and Presto, so its SQL and functions follow Trino’s. It reads and writes Iceberg tables, with INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, OPTIMIZE and time travel, and it reads Delta Lake and Hudi tables. Federated Query connectors reach sources outside S3, such as DynamoDB and other databases.
strengths: Nothing to run or size: query S3 moments after defining a table
Pay only for data scanned, with no idle cost
Iceberg reads and writes, with Glue as the catalog and Lake Formation to manage read access
limits: Cost tracks bytes scanned, so a `SELECT *` over raw CSV or JSON gets expensive fast
Iceberg tables must use the Glue catalog and format v2, and timestamps are limited to millisecond precision
Delta Lake is read-only, with no time travel
Trino connectors and fault-tolerant execution aren’t available; outside sources go through Federated Query

story: By 2016, many people were querying structured and semi-structured files at petabyte scale. Asking a question of data in S3 still meant work first: preprocessing, scanning, loading or indexing it, and building, managing and tuning a cluster to query it. Their questions were often ad hoc and exploratory, and they wanted answers in minutes.

AWS announced Amazon Athena at re:Invent on November 30, 2016. In his launch post, Jeff Barr described the goal as letting people run queries and act on the results “all in a matter of minutes”, without spending time on “preprocessing, scanning, loading, or indexing data”. Athena was based on Facebook’s open-source Presto engine. You defined a table with SQL DDL pointing at files in S3 (CSV, JSON, logs, Parquet or ORC) and queried them in place. There was no cluster to build, manage or tune, and you paid only for the data each query scanned. It launched in two regions.

Later releases added the Glue Data Catalog as a shared table registry, federated queries to other databases, Iceberg tables with row-level changes, and reserved capacity for steady workloads. In 2022 engine version 3 brought in the latest features from Trino, the project Presto’s creators renamed from PrestoSQL in 2020.

choices.choice: Build on open-source Presto rather than a new engine
choices.why: Presto had already run interactive SQL over petabytes at Facebook and read files in place, a natural fit for data sitting in S3. Engine version 3 now pulls in Trino and Presto changes continuously.

choices.choice: Bill per byte scanned, not per server
choices.why: Ad-hoc queries are bursty, so paying for idle clusters made no sense. Charging by data scanned also rewards compressing, partitioning and converting data to columnar formats, which AWS recommended from launch.

choices.choice: Schema on read over files in S3
choices.why: A table is just a definition pointing at files, so there is nothing to load or index: data written by any tool can be queried as soon as it lands.

timeline.text: Announced at re:Invent on November 30, based on Presto
Integrates with the new AWS Glue Data Catalog
Federated Query reaches general availability in November, with connectors on Lambda
Iceberg ACID transactions GA in April; engine version 3, with the latest Trino features, in October
Provisioned Capacity offers fixed-price compute instead of per-TB billing
Capacity reservations can be bought by the minute, from 4 DPUs
